description: We are a one-person team. I'm an automation developer who builds web applications with AI-assisted tools. For the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge, I will build a browser-based game where kids aged 7-12 run a base on Mars and learn real engineering trade-offs by playing, grounded in NASA open data. Like a commander's logbook, every sol of the mission is recorded. We are not looking for new members at this time.
summary:
Seyir Defteri: The Last 30 Sols ("Seyir Defteri" is Turkish for "Ship's Log") is a free 3D browser game for children aged 7-12. Play it now, no download and no account: https://saidbilaldariyemez.github.io/seyir-defteri/

Your rocket crash-lands near Gale Crater on Mars. With PUSULA, a friendly robot, the child builds a small base and keeps the crew safe for 30 sols until the rescue ship lands. No choice is free: every task costs daylight hours, power or oxygen. Power spent in the day is missing for the night heating; waiting in the radiation shelter keeps the dose low but stops the work; a message to Earth takes minutes each way, so in an emergency you decide.

The storms are real. Storm warnings come from the NASA DONKI space-weather events of the played month, and the radiation dose follows Curiosity's real RAD measurements hour by hour (via NASA OSDR RadLab), including the storm of 20 May 2024, the biggest one Curiosity has measured. At the end the child sees "This storm was real" with the actual RAD curve.

Children usually see a mission's result, never the trade-offs behind it. Here they make the trade-offs themselves and see what happens that same night. A headless bot played 4,200 games to prove that no single strategy wins for free.
details:
▶ Play it yourself

  • Live game: https://saidbilaldariyemez.github.io/seyir-defteri/ (runs in any modern browser, no download, no account, English / Turkish; the first sol is a guided tutorial)
  • Source code (MIT): https://github.com/SAIDBILALDARIYEMEZ/seyir-defteri
  • Demo deck (7 slides): https://saidbilaldariyemez.github.io/seyir-defteri/seyir-defteri-demo-en.pdf

Screenshots from the real game (not AI-generated): the crew waits in the shelter during the real storm of 20 May 2024; the night card with "Today → Tomorrow"; "This storm was real" with Curiosity's RAD curve.

Team

Team "Seyir Defteri" (Ship's Log), Local Event: Antalya, Turkey. Challenge: Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer.

  • Said Bilal Darıyemez: founder and team lead
  • Yahya Yılmaz

The challenge we answered

The challenge asks for a game in which young learners run a Martian or lunar outpost and balance life support, radiation shielding, power and food, so that they feel the decisions that make a mission succeed or fail. Each goal has a concrete place in the game:

  • Life support: an oxygen machine (modelled on NASA's MOXIE) makes oxygen; the crew breathes some every night. A cold night (not enough power for heating) drains extra oxygen.
  • Radiation shielding: a regolith shelter. The storm dose comes from Curiosity's real RAD measurements; waiting in the shelter keeps it low but costs working time.
  • Energy budget: solar panels work only in daylight and lose power as dust settles; the night heating takes its share. Power spent in the day is missing at night.
  • Food: the greenhouse needs care; the food store has a limit, so harvesting too much is wasted.
  • Communication delay: the message card shows the one-way delay for the played date (about 3-22 minutes, computed from the Earth-Mars distance) and the round trip. PUSULA: "Earth is far away; in an emergency you decide." The answer arrives the next morning.
  • No free choice: every action costs daylight hours, and making oxygen, building and heating cost power. Doing everything is impossible in one sol, so every day is a trade-off.
  • Two or three core resources: the dashboard shows three big gauges, power, oxygen and storm dose; food, parts and science are smaller.

How it works

Story. A rocket crash-lands near Gale Crater, Mars (Curiosity's real landing area, 4.6° S 137.4° E). The astronaut Ada and PUSULA ("compass" in Turkish), a friendly robot, must keep the crew safe for 30 sols until a rescue ship lands. Failure is never shown as harm: the crew takes an "Early Evacuation" capsule, and the game says "Every commander learns this way."

Game loop (one sol).

  1. Morning: PUSULA's wrist watch lists the day's tasks in priority order and keeps only what fits the daylight left.
  2. Day: the child taps a station, Ada walks there and works. Each action shows its cost (hours, power) and its result as icons. New buildings are dragged from the store onto the valley (a green ghost means "good spot"), are paid with parts and take sols to build.
  3. Night: a night card shows "Today → Tomorrow" in one line, then what the panels made, what the night heating, breathing and dinner took, the dust and the storm dose. If something went wrong, PUSULA explains why (see Learning design).

Daylight, power and night heating. Daylight hours are the main budget. Panels gather less and less power as dust settles, so cleaning them is a recurring chore. Every point of power used in the day is missing at night; a cold night costs extra oxygen. The child learns to keep a reserve.

Storms and the shelter. Warnings come from the real solar events of the played month (DONKI). When a particle storm reaches Mars, the dose rises with Curiosity's real hour-by-hour RAD rate. Waiting in the shelter protects the crew but stops all outside work. The Curiosity spot acts as a "storm radar" for tomorrow; the card labels this as a game simplification. Dust storms are shown separately: they dim the panels but are not radiation.

Antenna and rescue. The rescue needs a chain: build the antenna → contact Earth → send the landing coordinates → rescue landing. Without the antenna there is no rescue.

Exploring. Pieces of the crashed rocket lie around the crater; collecting them gives spare parts for upgrades (a bigger food store, an extra solar panel).

Three real months. May 2024 (the biggest storm Curiosity has measured, on 20 May), September 2017 (a classic solar storm, also felt on Mars) and March 2023 (storms hit Earth while Mars stayed calm). After the first win the child can pick the month.

Learning design

  • The 5 hazards of human spaceflight (NASA Human Research Program): every building teaches one: shelter → radiation, antenna → isolation, oxygen machine / greenhouse / landing marker → distance from Earth, habitat / panels → hostile closed environment; gravity is part of the whole mission.
  • Spaced recall, never graded: short knowledge capsules appear at natural moments (at most one per sol). On every 4th showing of a concept, PUSULA asks an optional fill-the-gap question: three big buttons, no timer, no penalty, "Skip" always available; a wrong answer shows the right one with the explanation. Concepts: sol, MOXIE, regolith, solar flare / CME, RAD, Gale Crater, message delay, Curiosity.
  • "Why did it happen?" After a mistake, PUSULA's night note gives three short lines: what happened → why → next time (for example: time spent outside during a storm, tasks left undone again, the day ended early, oxygen or harvest wasted because the store was full). Never blaming.
  • "Today → Tomorrow": the night card opens with one big cause-and-effect line, so the child links today's choice to tomorrow's situation.
  • Replay yesterday (3 times per mission): try the other choice and compare.
  • "This storm was real": at the end, the real RAD curve of the storm, the child's dose that sol, and what-ifs (habitat only, full shelter), with the data source and date.
  • Plain language: one short sentence per card, icons first; details open with a tap (ℹ️). Words such as sol, RAD, regolith and dose are underlined; a tap explains them in one sentence.
  • Rank and XP: Cadet → Rookie → Specialist → Commander → Mission Legend; XP for building, collecting parts, sheltering during a storm and correct answers.
  • Class mission code: a 6-character code. Everyone with the same code plays the same storms, so a class can compare choices and results.

Testing and results

Input → output. The simulation is a pure, deterministic function, (state, action, seeded random, month data) → new state, with no graphics code inside it. The same seed and month always give the same game. This lets a headless bot play the real game rules in Node.

Bot test: 7 strategies × 3 real months × 200 games = 4,200 games per run, repeated after every balance change. Win rates (May 2024, the big-storm month):

  • Follow PUSULA's advice: 94.5% win
  • Balanced: 81.0% (29% reach "Mission Legend")
  • Always shelter: 17.5% (runs out of oxygen)
  • Greedy (work as much as possible): 4.5%
  • Random: 0.5%
  • Never shelter: 0% (99.5% end by storm dose)
  • Never build the antenna: 0% (no rescue signal)

In the calm months "never shelter" wins 86.5% (September 2017 and March 2023), as in reality: the shelter matters only when a storm really reaches Mars. What we learned: no strategy wins for free; the best plan follows the real data of the month. Our balance targets (balanced ≥ 70%, following PUSULA ≥ 80%, never shelter in May 2024 ≤ 30%, random ≤ 20%) are all met. 83 unit tests cover the simulation, saves and data adapters.

Experiments we reverted (the bot told us):

  • A power cost for every action (cleaning, shelter building, reading Curiosity, scanning rocks, repairs): in round 1 the balanced player won only 0-0.5%, in round 2 18-24%, because every point spent in the day is missing for the night heating. We reverted it and kept time (daylight hours) as the cost of those actions.
  • Charging a cost for every missed task dropped the balanced win rate to about 57% and "Mission Legend" to almost 0; now only a task that was already overdue and is left undone again costs something.
  • Collecting all rocket pieces in one go made the game too easy (100% wins), so it is one piece per sol.

Real players and mentor. Two rounds of play tests with test players and our mentor's feedback gave the same message: too much text. We rebuilt the interface for ages 7-12: one sentence per card plus icons, details only in tap pop-ups, one dashboard strip with three big gauges, PUSULA as a face with three moods (happy, worried, alarm), icon tiles in the store, a mini map, and the night card's "Today → Tomorrow" line. Earlier test feedback also gave us walk retargeting, autosave and saved games, a task list that fits the daylight, and clearer shelter waiting.

Accessibility

  • Runs in a web browser on laptops, tablets and classroom smart boards; no download, no account, no personal data collected (progress is saved only on the device).
  • English and Turkish, switchable in the settings.
  • Smart board friendly: big buttons (≥ 64 px on learning cards), large text option ("Text size: large").
  • "Reduce motion" setting (follows the system setting by default): no camera shake, no flashes or blinking.
  • Sound can be turned off.
  • Icons together with numbers, so the dashboard can be read without much reading.

Tools and technology

TypeScript (strict), Vite, three.js (3D), Vitest (unit tests), Node.js (headless playtest bot and data fetch scripts), Web Audio API (all sounds are synthesized in code, no audio files), Draco (model compression). Static hosting on GitHub Pages. Low-poly CC0 3D models (KayKit, Quaternius). About 12,700 lines of TypeScript; simulation, scene and interface are separate layers.

Use of NASA data (summary; full links in the NASA Data field)

  • DONKI (Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information): SEP, CME, GST and flare notifications. In the game: the storm warnings of each played month come from that month's real events (SAVED snapshot, date shown). The main menu card "Today on the Sun" shows the last 7 days LIVE from the DONKI API (6-second timeout; on failure it falls back to the SAVED copy and shows its date). Why: real warnings make the storm story true.
  • Curiosity RAD (MSL Radiation Assessment Detector) via NASA OSDR RadLab: surface dose rate measured in Gale Crater. In the game: stored as hourly means for each month; it drives the storm dose (only the rate above the month's median counts, scaled to the game's dose gauge, which is labelled as a game simplification), the shelter decision, PUSULA's storm advice, the storm radar and the "This storm was real" chart. SAVED only (the service has no browser access), with the date on every card. Why: it is the only direct measurement of radiation on the surface of Mars.
  • NASA mission facts (MOXIE, MSL Curiosity, InSight, Mars facts), NASA Human Research Program (5 hazards) and NASA OSDR study OSD-268 (lettuce grown on the ISS): one-sentence facts on cards and in PUSULA's capsules, in our own words.
  • JPL "Approximate Positions of the Planets": orbital elements used to compute the Earth-Mars distance and the radio delay for the played date. This is a calculation, not a dataset; the card says "about".
  • NASA 3D Resources: the Perseverance rover model as decoration at the valley edge (logo decals removed).

We never present static data as live. Every data card carries a SAVED or LIVE badge with its date. Game simplifications are labelled as such, and no invented number is shown as NASA data.

Use of AI

Concept, story, characters and game design decisions are by the team. Claude (Anthropic) was used as a coding assistant, for data research and proofreading. No AI-generated images, video or audio; cutscenes are rendered in-engine from CC0 models and sounds are synthesized in code. AI-assisted code is noted in the repository (every code file carries an assistance note). No NASA logo, flag or mission patch is used anywhere; agency names appear only as data sources, and the project is not endorsed by any space agency.

Limitations and next steps

  • One astronaut is controlled (the crew model is ready for more).
  • The dose gauge shows the storm dose only, scaled to a game budget; it is not total radiation.
  • Earth's reply arrives the next morning, always later than the real round trip; the storm radar "sees ahead", which real instruments cannot.
  • Three real months are included; RAD data is available only until June 2024.
  • Play testing was small and informal; we have not run a classroom study yet.
  • Next: decision cards with no single right answer, a power budget for every device (needs new balancing), crater exploration, mini games, more real months, and a Moon mission with lunar radiation data.
